NoteKey Finding



Farming postcodes consistently recorded lower broadband availability than urban areas and generally performed worse than surrounding rural settlements, particularly for high-speed and gigabit services.

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Background and Aim
Farming communities are often geographically isolated and may face additional barriers to accessing services that are increasingly delivered online. This analysis uses open geospatial and administrative data to investigate whether likely farming locations experience poorer broadband connectivity than surrounding rural communities and urban areas across the UK.

“Access to services is getting harder — everything is further away, and more of it is online. Without decent internet or phone signal, farmers are at a real disadvantage. Farmhouses often sit further out than other rural homes, which means poorer broadband and longer journeys for even simple services. Poor connectivity isn’t just inconvenient; it creates real barriers to healthcare, work and basic communication for farming families.”

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Why this Matters
Access to many public and private services now depends on digital connectivity. Communities with poor broadband coverage may face barriers to:

Healthcare
Education
Employment
Government services
Business activity
Social participation

As more services move online, differences in connectivity may contribute to wider inequalities in access to opportunities and support.

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Methods
This analysis combines several open datasets:

OFCOM Connected Nations 2025 broadband data
ONS Postcode Directory active postcodes
UK urban-rural classifications
OpenStreetMap farmyard features
Companies House agricultural business records

Broadband indicators were linked at postcode level and compared across urban, rural and likely farming locations. Spatial analysis was used to assess whether patterns of connectivity cluster geographically.

Urban and Rural Classifications
The UK does not currently have a single harmonised urban-rural classification covering all four nations. England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland each publish slightly different classification systems based on their own definitions and census geographies.
For this analysis, official classifications from each nation were combined into a common UK-wide urban/rural framework. This enabled comparisons across the whole UK while acknowledging that alternative classification approaches are available and may produce slightly different results.

Urban-Rural Classification Harmonisation Method



Identifying Farming Locations
There is currently no open national register of farm properties in the UK.
Likely farm locations were identified by combining OpenStreetMap farmyard features with Companies House records for agricultural businesses. While this approach is not perfect and may miss some farms, it provides a reproducible method for identifying farming postcodes using open data.
(See Methods - Identifying Locations)

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Key Findings

Farming Locations Remain Among the Least Connected
Broadband availability was consistently lower for farming postcodes than for either urban or rural locations.
The differences were modest when considering minimum service levels but became much larger for higher-speed broadband services.


The Gap Widens at Higher Broadband Speeds

USO (Universal Service Obligation) refers to the UK’s minimum broadband service standard of 10 Mb/s download speed.
The largest differences emerge when considering access to high-speed and gigabit-capable broadband services. While basic connectivity is widespread, access to faster infrastructure becomes progressively less common in rural and farming locations.

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Gigabit Broadband Availability, UK


*Data sources: OFCOM, ONS, OpenStreetMap

Rural Classifications Can Hide Important Differences
Official statistics already show a rural-urban divide in connectivity.
However, this analysis suggests that broad rural classifications may conceal important variation within rural areas. Farming communities often experience poorer broadband availability than neighbouring villages despite both being classified as rural.


Broadband Access is Geographically Clustered
Areas with good broadband connectivity tend to be located near other well-connected areas, while poorly connected areas also occur together geographically.



Indicator
Moran’s I




Above USO

≥30 Mb/s

Gigabit Availability

The stronger clustering observed for higher-speed broadband suggests that inequalities in access are not randomly distributed but instead reflect broader infrastructure patterns.

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Interpretation
The findings broadly support existing evidence that rural areas experience poorer digital connectivity than urban areas.
They also suggest that farming households may experience additional disadvantage beyond that reflected in national rural averages. As services continue to move online, poorer broadband access may create barriers to participation in economic and social life.

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Limitations






Important



There is currently no open national register of farm properties in the UK.


Several limitations should be considered:

Farm locations were estimated using open data sources
Some active farms may not have been identified
Postcode centroids were used rather than postcode boundaries
Broadband data are reported at postcode level
Comparable mobile coverage data were not available at a similar spatial scale

Results should therefore be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive.

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Future Research
Potential extensions include:

Deprivation and digital exclusion
Mobile coverage and signal quality
Household-level analysis through UPRN linkage
Distance to telecommunications infrastructure
Comparison of alternative urban-rural classifications
Development of a harmonised UK-wide rural classification framework

A better understanding of within-rural variation may help identify communities most at risk of digital exclusion.

title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Farm internet speeds remain among the lowest in the country despite increasing dependence on digital services.



Access to services is increasingly digital. From healthcare and education to banking and government services, many everyday activities now depend on a reliable internet connection.
Communities with poor connectivity may face barriers to participation in modern society.





Farming postcodes consistently recorded poorer internet connectivity than urban areas and generally performed worse than surrounding rural settlements, particularly when looking at higher-speed broadband services.

Access to broadband appears closely linked to infrastructure. Urban areas benefit from greater coverage, while connectivity decreases in more remote and dispersed settlements.
Farms often occupy the most geographically isolated locations and experience lower access to faster services.


The analysis suggests that broad urban-rural classifications may mask important differences within rural areas.
Farming communities often experience poorer connectivity than neighbouring villages despite both being classified as rural.

This analysis therefore identifies likely farming locations using a combination of:

Use of postcode centroids rather than boundaries
Postcode-level broadband data
No comparable mobile coverage data at postcode scale
